newsitem.title: FRANCE: Adjani-led jury to award Cannes Golden Palm award.
newsitem.headline: Adjani-led jury to award Cannes Golden Palm award.

text.p: The Cannes festival jury was due to award the Golden Palm on Sunday at a prize-giving ceremony ending a 50th birthday edition overshadowed by on-screen violence and off-screen censorship.

Most critics at the French Riviera resort saw no outright favourite for the money-spinning top prize, which was to be awarded by the jury headed by French actress Isaebelle Adjani at a gala starting at 7.15 p.m. (1715 GMT).

"Quality-wise this year has been very average. Just a few years ago, and even more so 20 years ago, there was a masterpiece a day at the festival," Michel Ciment, who edits the French film magazine Positif, told Reuters.
Surveys by Screen International and Moving Pictures put Ang Lee's "The Ice Storm" about a New York suburban family and Curtis Hanson's fast-paced thriller "LA Confidential" in a narrow lead.

Outsiders also tipped by Cannes critics to pick up big prizes include Gary Oldman's partly-autobiographical "Nil By Mouth" on his East London roots, and Michael Winterbottom's "Welcome To Sarajevo" on a television journalist's adoption of a Bosnian child.

Ciment opted for Canadian-raised Atom Egoyan's film "The Sweet Hereafter", because it "is very rich and complex, and because it's his seventh film and he's at the stage where he needs a major reward."

The film is a gripping account of a small British Columbia town coping with a school bus accident, in which British actor Ian Holm pulls off an impressive performance as the devil's advocate -- an ambulance-chasing lawyer seeking to reap the bitter harvest.
Violence in many films -- sci-fi in French director Luc Besson's "The Fifth Element" or wife-beating in Oldman's movie, among others -- dampened birthday celebrations.

The anniversary was further dulled by Chinese censors stopping both Zhang Yimou and Zhang Yuan from coming to Cannes. French President Jacques Chirac, basking in free publicity ahead of the May-June general election, visited Cannes for the 50th anniversary and then flew to China to sign business contracts.
Director Abbas Kiarostami of Iran was given the green light to come to the festival only at the last minute and was given a standing ovation at his screening of "The Taste of the Cherry".
"What is serious this year is that there were no major discoveries outside the competition, no one like Wim Wenders for example," Ciment said.

"This year there was too much of an emphasis on stars. There were much better films for the competition than Johnny Depp's 'The Brave' but organisers wanted him and possibly Marlon Brando so it got in," he said.

To the relief of festival-goers, Clint Eastwood's closing film "Absolute Power", shown out of competition, produced the goods so many entries failed to come up with -- a pacy and credible story, reliable acting and some hilarious moments.

Typically of Eastwood it pits an invididual with moral standards, in this case a thief, against evil in the form of the President of the United States desperate to cover up his involvement in a mistress's murder.
